name: Hexagon quilt

summary: Give the Hexagon quilt calculator the width of quilt, the length of quilt and the size of hexagon and it returns number of hexagonal columns. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Hexagon quilt calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hexagon quilt calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of hexagonal columns in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the width of quilt, the length of quilt and the size of hexagon.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hexagon quilt calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of hexagonal columns=rounded up, ((250 ÷ 433) × width of quilt ÷ size of hexagon)
Number of hexagonal rows=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 3) × (-size of hexagon + 2 × length of quilt) ÷ size of hexagon)
Number of hexagons=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 3) × (size of hexagon × (2 − rounded up, ((250 ÷ 433) × width of quilt ÷ size of hexagon)) + 2 × length of quilt × rounded up, ((250 ÷ 433) × width of quilt ÷ size of hexagon) − length of quilt) ÷ size of hexagon)
Number of half hexagons=rounded up, ((2 ÷ 3) × (-2 × size of hexagon + length of quilt) ÷ size of hexagon)
Actual width=(433 ÷ 250) × size of hexagon × rounded up, ((250 ÷ 433) × width of quilt ÷ size of hexagon)
Actual length=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 2) × size of hexagon × (3 × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 3) × (-size of hexagon + 2 × length of quilt) ÷ size of hexagon) + 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Width of quilt = 30 cm and Size of hexagon = 30 cm. Working through the relationship above gives Number of hexagonal columns = 1 and Actual width = 51.96 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of hexagonal columns = 1 and Actual width = 51.96 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Width of quilt = 30 cm and Size of hexagon = 30 cm.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hexagon quilt calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the width of quilt, the length of quilt and the size of hexagon — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hexagon quilt calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of hexagonal columns, derived from the width of quilt, the length of quilt and the size of hexagon. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hexagon quilt calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the width of quilt, the length of quilt and the size of hexagon, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter width of quilt in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Width of quilt opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of hexagonal columns = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hexagon quilt calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
